message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"4.11","text":"There is a great difference, men of Greece, between truth and custom. Truth, when genuinely sought, is found; but a custom, whatever form it has when received, whether true or false, is uncritically reinforced by itself. The person who has received it neither delights in it because it is true nor is distressed because it is false. For such a person has believed not through judgment but through preconception, entrusting his own hope, with the outcome uncertain, to the opinion of those before him. And it is not easy to strip off the ancestral garment, even if it is shown to him quite plainly to be foolish and ridiculous.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀληθείας τε καὶ συνηθείας","chosen":"truth and custom","rationale":"συνήθεια can denote familiarity, habit, or customary practice; the ensuing discussion of inherited ἔθος supports “custom.”"},{"source_quote":"τὸ δὲ ἔθος, ὁποῖον ἂν παραληφθῇ","chosen":"but a custom, whatever form it has when received","rationale":"The rendering preserves both the indefinite quality of ὁποῖον and the idea of receiving an established custom."},{"source_quote":"ἀκρίτως ὑφ’ ἑαυτοῦ κρατύνεται","chosen":"is uncritically reinforced by itself","rationale":"The reflexive agent is retained rather than assigning the reinforcement to an unstated external authority."},{"source_quote":"οὐ γὰρ κρίσει, ἀλλὰ προλήψει","chosen":"not through judgment but through preconception","rationale":"πρόληψις here is a belief accepted in advance rather than a conclusion reached by critical judgment; “presupposition” or “prejudice” are possible alternatives."},{"source_quote":"τὴν πάτριον περιβολήν","chosen":"the ancestral garment","rationale":"The concrete clothing image of περιβολή is preserved rather than flattened to “ancestral tradition.”"}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"4.12","text":"For example, then, I say that the entire education of the Greeks is a most pernicious scheme of an evil demon. Some of them introduced many gods, and these evil and subject to every passion, so that anyone wishing to do similar things might not even feel shame—shame being characteristic of a human being—since he has as his example the evil and indecent lives of the gods spoken of in myth. And by not even feeling shame, such a person shows no hope of reorientation. Others introduced fate, the so-called nativity, contrary to which no one can experience or do anything. So this too is likewise the same as the first position. For when someone has come to believe that no one is able either to experience or to do anything contrary to nativity, he readily comes to sin—and after sinning he does not regret what he has done impiously, offering as a defense that he was forced by nativity to do these things—and, since he is unable to correct his nativity, he is not even capable of feeling shame for the ways in which he sins.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὴν πᾶσαν Ἑλλήνων παιδείαν κακοῦ δαίμονος χαλεπωτάτην ὑπόθεσιν","chosen":"the entire education of the Greeks is a most pernicious scheme of an evil demon","rationale":"παιδεία denotes the Greek system of education or culture, while ὑπόθεσις here is understood as an underlying scheme or design; “most grievous undertaking” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"παντοπαθεῖς","chosen":"subject to every passion","rationale":"The word characterizes the gods as undergoing or being governed by every kind of passion, not merely as suffering greatly."},{"source_quote":"ὅπερ ἐστὶν ἀνθρώπου ἴδιον","chosen":"shame being characteristic of a human being","rationale":"ὅπερ is taken as referring to the immediately relevant act of feeling shame; reference to the broader preceding clause is grammatically possible but less fitting in context."},{"source_quote":"ἐλπίδα μετανοίας","chosen":"hope of reorientation","rationale":"μετάνοια denotes the prospect of moral redirection here. The traditional alternative is “hope of repentance”; no Godward destination is added because the clause does not specify one."},{"source_quote":"τὴν λεγομένην γένεσιν","chosen":"the so-called nativity","rationale":"In this argument γένεσις is the astrologically determined condition associated with one’s birth, not simply the event of birth; “birth-destiny” is an explanatory alternative."},{"source_quote":"παρ’ ἣν μηδένα πάσχειν τι ἢ ποιεῖν δύνασθαι","chosen":"contrary to which no one can experience or do anything","rationale":"παρά with the accusative is read as “contrary to” or “outside the determination of”; “apart from which” is a viable alternative."},{"source_quote":"τὴν γένεσιν κατορθῶσαι μὴ δυνάμενος","chosen":"since he is unable to correct his nativity","rationale":"κατορθόω can mean set right, correct, or successfully master. “Correct” preserves the text’s deliberately impossible task without replacing it with an explanatory paraphrase."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"4.13","text":"Others propose a motion devoid of providence, as though all things revolved spontaneously, with no master presiding over them. To think this way about these matters, as we have said, is in fact the most pernicious of all beliefs. For, as though there were no one presiding, exercising providence, and assigning to each person what is deserved, someone will readily do everything he can because of his lack of fear. Hence those who think such things are not easily—or perhaps not at all—brought to self-restraint, for they do not foresee the danger that would turn them back. But the teaching of the barbarian Jews, as you call them, is most pious, proposing one Father and Creator of this universe, good and just by nature: good, in that he forgives the sins of those who regret them; and just, in that after the reorientation he proceeds against each person according to what the things done deserve.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀπρονόητον φορὰν","chosen":"a motion devoid of providence","rationale":"φορά can denote motion, course, or movement; the following description of everything revolving spontaneously favors cosmic “motion.”"},{"source_quote":"διὰ τὴν ἀφοβίαν","chosen":"because of his lack of fear","rationale":"This avoids the potentially positive connotations of English “fearlessness” and expresses the absence of deterrent fear intended by the argument."},{"source_quote":"τὸν γὰρ ἐπιστρέφοντα κίνδυνον","chosen":"the danger that would turn them back","rationale":"ἐπιστρέφοντα is taken transitively, with the affected persons understood. “The returning danger” or “the danger coming back upon them” is also grammatically possible."},{"source_quote":"μεταμελομένοις χαριζόμενον τὰ ἁμαρτήματα","chosen":"he forgives the sins of those who regret them","rationale":"χαρίζομαι with sins means freely remit or forgive them. μεταμέλομαι is rendered with regret rather than the distinct reorientation terminology used for μετάνοια."},{"source_quote":"μετὰ τὴν μετάνοιαν","chosen":"after the reorientation","rationale":"The temporal force of μετά is retained, even though this wording creates tension with the preceding statement about forgiveness. Alternatives include “after the change of mind” and the traditional “after repentance”; it is not rewritten as “if there is no reorientation.”"},{"source_quote":"ἑκάστῳ ... κατ’ ἀξίαν τῶν πεπραγμένων ἐπεξιόντα","chosen":"he proceeds against each person according to what the things done deserve","rationale":"ἐπεξέρχομαι with the dative can mean proceed against, pursue, or call someone to account. “Proceeds against” retains its judicial and potentially punitive force without supplying a different verb such as “reward.”"}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ὡς. αὐτομάτως","issue":"The confirmed printed period after ὡς interrupts a construction in which ὡς introduces the following description. The translation treats the stop as editorial punctuation rather than as the end of an independent sentence.","proposed_reading":"ὡς, αὐτομάτως","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ταῦτα δὲ οὕτω νομίζειν, ὡς εἰρήκαμεν, πασῶν δοξῶν τυγχάνει οὖσα χαλεπωτάτη","issue":"The feminine forms οὖσα χαλεπωτάτη do not formally agree with the neuter infinitival clause ταῦτα ... νομίζειν. The sentence remains intelligible as an anacoluthon or as attraction to an understood feminine δόξα, “belief,” but no unique grammatical repair is certain.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"4.14","text":"This teaching, even if it happens to be a myth, would nevertheless, since it is at least pious, not be unprofitable for life. For each person, in expectation of being judged by the all-seeing God, receives a stronger impulse toward self-restraint. And if the teaching should also be true, it has delivered the one who has lived with self-restraint from eternal punishment and has additionally benefited him through the everlasting and ineffable good things provided by God.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"οὗτος ὁ λόγος","chosen":"this teaching","rationale":"λόγος here denotes the religious account or doctrine described in the preceding section, not merely a spoken word."},{"source_quote":"εὐσεβής γε ὢν","chosen":"since it is at least pious","rationale":"γε gives concessive emphasis: even if the teaching were a myth, its pious character would still make it beneficial."},{"source_quote":"τοῦ παντεπόπτου θεοῦ","chosen":"the all-seeing God","rationale":"παντεπόπτης describes one who observes everything; “all-observing God” is a close alternative."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς τὸ σωφρονεῖν","chosen":"toward self-restraint","rationale":"σωφρονεῖν here concerns morally disciplined conduct. “Sound-mindedness” or “temperance” would preserve other aspects of the term."},{"source_quote":"προσευεργέτηκεν δὲ τοῖς ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀιδίοις τε καὶ ἀπορρήτοις γιγνομένοις ἀγαθοῖς","chosen":"has additionally benefited him through the everlasting and ineffable good things provided by God","rationale":"The dative τοῖς ... ἀγαθοῖς is taken instrumentally, and the beneficiary is supplied from the preceding τὸν σωφρόνως βεβιωκότα. “Has further bestowed benefit on him with” is a more formal alternative."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"κριθήσεσθαι. ὑπὸ","issue":"The confirmed printed period separates the passive infinitive κριθήσεσθαι from its agent phrase ὑπὸ τοῦ παντεπόπτου θεοῦ. The syntax requires them to be construed together, so the translation does not reproduce the disruptive stop.","proposed_reading":"κριθήσεσθαι ὑπὸ","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"4.15","text":"Nevertheless, I return to the first belief of the Greeks, the one that tells the myth that there are many gods subject to every passion. And so that I may not spend much time on settled matters by setting out the impious deeds of each of the so-called gods, I would not, for my part, recount all their love affairs: those of Zeus and Poseidon, Pluto and Apollo, Dionysus and Heracles, and of every one of them individually. Not even you yourselves are ignorant of their lives, since you proceed from a Greek education—the lives in which you were instructed so that, as emulators of the gods, you might do similar things,","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὴν πρωτίστην τῶν Ἑλλήνων δόξαν","chosen":"the first belief of the Greeks","rationale":"πρωτίστην is read contextually as the first position previously listed, namely belief in many gods. “Foremost belief” or “earliest belief” is also lexically possible."},{"source_quote":"τὴν πολλοὺς καὶ παντοπαθεῖς θεοὺς εἶναι μυθολογοῦσαν","chosen":"the one that tells the myth that there are many gods subject to every passion","rationale":"The participle μυθολογοῦσαν characterizes the belief as narrating or asserting through myth, while παντοπαθεῖς retains the gods’ subjection to every passion."},{"source_quote":"εἰς τὰ ἀσφαλῆ","chosen":"on settled matters","rationale":"ἀσφαλής here describes matters treated as certain or already established, not physically safe things."},{"source_quote":"πάντας ... αὐτῶν τοὺς ἔρωτας","chosen":"all their love affairs","rationale":"In the context of the gods’ indecent lives, ἔρωτες denotes their erotic involvements rather than love in a general sense."},{"source_quote":"ἐκ παιδείας Ἑλληνικῆς ὁρμώμενοι","chosen":"since you proceed from a Greek education","rationale":"ὁρμάομαι ἐκ marks one’s starting point or basis. “Being grounded in Greek education” is a smoother alternative."},{"source_quote":"οὓς ἐπαιδεύθητε βίους","chosen":"the lives in which you were instructed","rationale":"The compressed construction can describe lives or ways of life received as the content of education. Alternatives include “the lives you were taught” and “the ways of life in which you were trained.”"}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἵνα ὡς ζηλωταὶ τῶν θεῶν τὰ ὅμοια πράττοτε,","issue":"The selected section ends with a printed comma and therefore closes while the larger sentence or rhetorical sequence is still continuing. The English retains an open-ended close and supplies no continuation from outside the requested passage.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]}]}
